kenilworth.s1_head: Charity and volunteer kit in Kenilworth
s1loc: Kenilworth's charity life leans on Warwick District Foodbank, which grew from the volunteer-led Kenilworth food bank founded by local churches in 2012 and now serves Kenilworth, Warwick and Leamington from its warehouse and distribution centres. Compassionate Kenilworth coordinates support alongside Kenilworth Lions, Kenilworth Rotarians, the Round Table and the Soroptimists, with Lions volunteers running weekly warehouse sessions. The town's community pantries and church-run projects sit beside this network, feeding people in crisis across the district every week.

The sector here runs at every size. National and regional charities keep shops on Warwick Road, drawing on central buying and trade accounts, while small community groups, the foodbank's church-hosted sessions and volunteer-run drives work on a shoestring across Kenilworth's neighbourhoods. We are set up to serve the national charity with shops across the district and the one-room foodbank alike, with trade accounts for the big buyers and direct online ordering, no minimum, for the smallest group.

Beyond the high street, Kenilworth supports a wider weave of volunteer effort. Acorns Children's Hospice and The Myton Hospices raise funds through their Warwick Road stores and donated stock, while Age UK Warwickshire backs older residents across Bedworth, Bulkington, Studley and Rugby as well as Kenilworth. Mutual-aid and befriending groups, Rotary and Lions food drives at local supermarkets, and church-hosted community pantries fill the gaps, all staffed by townsfolk giving their time across Abbey End, Mortimer Road and the surrounding streets.

buxton.s1_head: Charity and volunteer kit in Buxton
s1loc: Buxton's voluntary sector is anchored by Connex Community Support, the charity that began as a Buxton Volunteer Bureau in the 1980s, merged with Volunteer Centre Derbyshire Dales, and now runs befriending, transport, home-from-hospital and digital-inclusion services with more than 250 volunteers across the High Peak and Derbyshire Dales. High Peak Foodbank, run at Zink, gives emergency food, fuel and housing help alongside advice, work coaching and wellbeing activities, while Vision Buxton and Buxton Street by Street rally local volunteers for the town's community projects.

The sector here runs at every size. National and regional charities keep shops along Spring Gardens and the town centre, drawing on central buying and trade accounts, while small community groups, the Zink foodbank parcel teams, church pantries and volunteer-run drives work on a shoestring across Buxton's districts and the wider High Peak. We are set up to serve the national charity with high-street shops and the one-room foodbank alike, with trade accounts for the big buyers and direct online ordering, no minimum, for the smallest group running on donations.

Around these anchors Buxton supports a broad volunteer network. Connex coordinates more than 26,000 volunteer hours a year for older and isolated residents, while Zink's work coaches, parcel-packers and advice workers tackle hardship at its roots. Charity shops, mutual-aid groups and church-hosted larders fill the gaps across Fairfield, Burbage and the town centre, and Voluntary and Community Services Peaks and Dales links smaller projects to funding and training. Vision Buxton's volunteer drives and town-centre events keep fresh hands flowing into the sector each year.

market harborough.s1_head: Charity and volunteer kit in Market Harborough
s1loc: Market Harborough's charity scene centres on Jubilee Foodbank Market Harborough, which works to relieve food poverty across the Harborough district and, in a single recent year, turned more than 1,000 referrals into over 23,000 meals through its Front Line Volunteers, Collections Team and Store Team. VASL, Voluntary Action South Leicestershire, is based in the town and provides advice, befriending and support for carers and older people living alone. A community fridge on St Mary's Road shares food and runs a kindness board for prepaid items.

The sector here runs at every size. National and regional charities keep shops in town - LOROS, the Leicestershire hospice charity, runs its Coventry Road store on central buying and trade accounts - while small community groups, the Jubilee Foodbank's collection points, church pantries and volunteer-run projects work on a shoestring across the district. We are set up to serve the national charity with shops across Market Harborough and the one-room foodbank alike, with trade accounts for the big buyers and direct online ordering, no minimum, for the smallest group.

Beyond the foodbank and the shops, the town supports a wider band of volunteers. LOROS draws on its hospice store and donated stock, VASL runs befriending and carer support from Welland Park and venues across the district, and Harborough District Council points residents to local volunteering through its community directory. Mutual-aid groups, church-hosted larders, the St Mary's Road community fridge and supermarket donation drives fill the gaps, staffed by townsfolk giving their time across Little Bowden, Logan Street and the surrounding villages each week.

garforth.s1_head: Charity and volunteer kit in Garforth
s1loc: Garforth sits within the reach of Leeds South and East Foodbank, part of the Trussell network, which runs distribution centres across the south and east of the city with a small paid team and well over 100 volunteers who weigh, sort and pack parcels and meet clients in crisis. Nearby centres such as St Wilfrid's Church on Selby Road show how church-hosted sessions reach the LS15 and LS25 communities. The Garforth Community Hub and library on Lidgett Lane add a base for local advice, signposting and volunteer-run activity.

The sector here runs at every size. National and regional charities keep shops along Main Street and across east Leeds, drawing on central buying and trade accounts, while small community groups, the foodbank's church-hosted sessions, pantries and volunteer-run drives work on a shoestring across Garforth's estates and the wider district. We are set up to serve the national charity with shops across Leeds and the one-room foodbank alike, with trade accounts for the big buyers and direct online ordering, no minimum, for the smallest group running on donations.

Around the foodbank and the hub, Garforth supports a steady weave of volunteer effort. FareShare Yorkshire rescues surplus food and supplies charities and community projects across Leeds, while the Leeds Food Aid Network links foodbanks, pantries and larders so help reaches people in need. Charity shops, church groups, mutual-aid networks and the Garforth Community Hub's volunteers fill the gaps across Barwick Road, Lidgett Lane and the neighbouring villages, with townsfolk giving their time to packing, collections and befriending throughout the year.

droylsden.s1_head: Charity and volunteer kit in Droylsden
s1loc: Droylsden's charity backbone is Droylsden and District Foodbank, set up under the Trussell umbrella in 2013 and run entirely by volunteers, with no paid staff, covering project management, distribution sessions, treasury and warehouse work. Supported by six Droylsden churches that supply both volunteers and donations, it fed over 1,700 people, including more than 700 children, in a recent year. Donations come in at the Droylsden Tesco store, and Action Together helps coordinate the wider Tameside voluntary sector with advice and support for small groups.

The sector here runs at every size. National and regional charities keep shops on Market Street and across Tameside, drawing on central buying and trade accounts, while small community groups, the foodbank's church-hosted sessions, pantries and volunteer-run drives work on a shoestring across Droylsden's neighbourhoods and the wider borough. We are set up to serve the national charity with shops across the town and the one-room foodbank alike, with trade accounts for the big buyers and direct online ordering, no minimum, for the smallest volunteer-run group.

Beyond the foodbank, Droylsden supports a broad band of volunteer effort. Willow Wood Hospice cares for Tameside and Glossop residents and runs six charity shops across the area plus a furniture shop and distribution centre, while the Tameside and Glossop Hospice Appeal shop sits on Market Street in Droylsden itself. Action Together links smaller groups to funding and training, and mutual-aid networks, church pantries and supermarket food drives fill the gaps across Fairfield, Audenshaw and the surrounding districts, staffed by local people giving their time week in, week out.

newquay.s1_head: Charity and volunteer kit in Newquay
s1loc: Newquay Foodbank, set up in 2011 to support the town and surrounding areas and working alongside the Trussell network, anchors the local charity scene, running sessions at St Columba Church in St Columb Minor, St Michael's Church in Newquay and the Oasis Centre in St Columb Major. It gives three days of food for people in crisis and runs a community larder alongside its parcels. FareShare South West rescues quality surplus food and supplies charities and community groups right across Cornwall, keeping shelves stocked at projects like these.

The sector here runs at every size. National and regional charities keep shops along Bank Street, drawing on central buying and trade accounts, while small community groups, the foodbank's church-hosted sessions, the community larder and volunteer-run drives work on a shoestring across Newquay's neighbourhoods and the wider area. We are set up to serve the national charity with shops across the town and the one-room foodbank alike, with trade accounts for the big buyers and direct online ordering, no minimum, for the smallest group running on donations.

Around the foodbank, Newquay supports a wide weave of volunteer effort. Churches Together in Cornwall backs the foodbank's church-hosted sessions, while the community larder, mutual-aid groups and church pantries fill the gaps across St Columb Minor, Pentire and the town centre. Charity shops raise funds for national and Cornish causes, supermarket donation drives keep stock flowing, and the foodbank's appeals for trustees and session volunteers draw fresh hands in. Local people give their time to packing, signposting and befriending right through the busy seasons each year.

truro.s1_head: Charity and volunteer kit in Truro
s1loc: Truro Foodbank, operating under the Trussell umbrella from Threemilestone Industrial Estate, anchors the city's charity scene, giving three days of emergency food to people in crisis and running sessions across the week where volunteers weigh, sort and store donated food, hand out parcels and signpost people to further support. The Cornwall Community Foundation has backed the foodbank through its emergency appeals, helping it feed more children than ever before, while Volunteer Cornwall recruits the rota and Christmas volunteers who keep it running.

The sector here runs at every size. National and regional charities keep shops across the city centre and Lemon Quay, drawing on central buying and trade accounts, while small community groups, the foodbank's Threemilestone sessions, pantries and volunteer-run drives work on a shoestring across Truro's neighbourhoods and the wider district. We are set up to serve the national charity with shops across the city and the one-room foodbank alike, with trade accounts for the big buyers and direct online ordering, no minimum, for the smallest group running on donations.

Beyond the foodbank, Truro supports a deep band of volunteer effort. FareShare South West rescues surplus food and supplies charities and community groups across Cornwall, the Cornwall Community Foundation channels grants to small local causes, and Volunteer Cornwall matches residents to roles right across the county. Charity shops, mutual-aid groups and church-hosted larders fill the gaps across Threemilestone, Highertown and the city centre, staffed by local people who give their time to packing, collections, signposting and befriending throughout the year.
